answers.answer: In case A, the 09:02 request can use the original cached copy because its five-minute lifetime has not ended, although the copy is stale after the source changes at 09:01. It expires at 09:05. At 09:06, expired entries cannot be served, so the API has a cache miss, reads the source, caches the returned copy, and returns it. In separate case B, removal at 09:03 is eviction to make room, which can happen before the 09:05 expiration. At 09:04 the original copy is absent, so the API must fetch the source and fill the cache. Removal itself does not fetch a replacement: in cache-aside the API performs the fetch on the later miss. A five-minute TTL does not promise five minutes of fresh data; it limits the entry lifetime, and a source change can make the entry stale earlier. evidence.quote: The entry is absent. The API reads the database, stores a copy in the cache, and returns the details.
A hit can still return an old price. Finding a value does not prove it matches the database.
The API checks and fills the cache explicitly. The cache does not fetch the product from the database on its own.
Sets how long an entry may remain before it expires. A 60-second TTL does not refresh the product every minute; a later miss must load it again.
Removes entries to make room. A least-recently-used policy favors removing entries that have not been read recently.
A product can be evicted before its TTL ends. Some configurations reject new entries when full instead of evicting existing ones.
TTL limits an entry's lifetime, not the age of the source data used to fill it.
